1: In six days God makes light, sky, land, plants, sun and stars, sea creatures, birds and animals, and finally man and woman in his own image. He sees that it is very good.
The world is not an accident and not divine; it is made by a good God. Every human being bears God's image.
2: The garden and the first marriage

God rests on the seventh day. He forms the man from dust, places him in Eden, and forbids one tree. No animal is a fit partner, so God makes the woman from the man's side, and the two become one flesh.
Work, rest and marriage come from God before sin enters. Man and woman are made for each other.
3: The serpent tempts the woman to doubt God. She and Adam eat the forbidden fruit, feel shame and hide. God questions them, pronounces the consequences, promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head, and sends them out of Eden.
This is the origin of original sin. Verse 15 is the first promise of a Saviour.
4: Both brothers bring offerings; God accepts Abel's. Cain kills Abel out of jealousy and asks, "Am I my brother's keeper?" God punishes Cain but puts a mark on him to protect him. Violence grows among his descendants.
Sin spreads quickly from disobedience to murder. Even then, God limits vengeance.
5: A list of ten generations, each ending with "and he died". Enoch walks with God and is taken by him. Methuselah lives 969 years. The line leads to Noah.
Death now rules the human story, as God warned. Enoch hints that it will not have the final word.
6: Human evil fills the earth and grieves God. Noah alone finds favour. God tells him to build an ark and bring in his family and pairs of every animal.
God takes evil seriously and also provides a way of rescue. Noah obeys in everything.
7: Noah, his family and the animals enter the ark. Rain falls forty days and the waters cover even the mountains. Everything outside the ark dies.
Peter sees the flood as a figure of baptism: judgement on sin and salvation through water.
8: God remembers Noah. The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and a dove, and the dove returns with an olive leaf. He leaves the ark and offers sacrifice.
God promises never again to destroy every living thing by flood. The seasons will continue.
9: God blesses Noah, forbids murder because man is made in God's image, and sets the rainbow as the sign of his covenant with all living things. Noah later gets drunk, and his son Ham dishonours him.
God commits himself to the whole of creation. Even the hero of the flood is still a sinner.
10: A list of the peoples descended from Noah's sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth, spread across the known world.
All nations belong to one human family.
11: People build a city and tower "to make a name for ourselves". God confuses their language and scatters them. The chapter then traces Shem's line down to Abram.
Pride divides humanity. Pentecost, where all understand one message, is the answer to Babel.
12: God tells Abram to leave his country and promises to make him a great nation through which all families of the earth will be blessed. Abram goes to Canaan. In Egypt, afraid for his life, he passes Sarai off as his sister.
The whole plan of salvation starts with one man who trusts and goes.
13: Their herds are too large to stay together. Abram lets Lot choose first; Lot takes the rich plain near Sodom. God renews the promise of land and descendants to Abram.
Abram is generous because he trusts God to provide.
14: Kings go to war and Lot is captured. Abram rescues him. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram.
The Church sees Melchizedek's bread and wine as a figure of the Eucharist and of Christ's priesthood.
15: Abram is childless. God shows him the stars and promises descendants as many. Abram believes, and it is counted to him as righteousness. God seals a covenant in a night vision.
Paul builds his teaching on faith on verse 6. God binds himself by oath.
16: Sarai, still barren, gives her servant Hagar to Abram. Hagar conceives, is mistreated and runs away. An angel meets her in the desert, and she bears Ishmael.
Trying to force God's promise causes pain. God sees the outcast.
17: God renames Abram "Abraham", father of many nations, and Sarai "Sarah". Circumcision becomes the sign of the covenant. God promises a son through Sarah within a year.
Circumcision marks belonging to God's people, as baptism does in the new covenant.
18: Abraham welcomes three strangers who announce that Sarah will bear a son. Sarah laughs. Then Abraham bargains with God for Sodom: will he spare it for ten just people?
"Is anything too hard for the Lord?" Abraham's bold prayer shows that intercession matters.
19: Two angels rescue Lot and his family before fire falls on the cities. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Lot's daughters later commit incest with him.
God judges grave sin and saves the just. Looking back longingly at sin is dangerous.
20: Abraham again says Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech takes her. God warns the king in a dream, and he returns her untouched.
God protects his promise in spite of Abraham's fear.
21: Sarah bears Isaac, the son of the promise. Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, and God cares for them in the desert. Abraham makes a treaty at Beersheba.
God keeps his word, even after twenty-five years of waiting.
22: God tests Abraham: offer your only son. Abraham obeys, Isaac carries the wood up the mountain, and at the last moment an angel stops the knife. A ram is offered instead.
A father offering his beloved son, who carries the wood, foreshadows Calvary. "God will provide the lamb."
23: Sarah dies. Abraham buys a field with a cave at Machpelah from the Hittites as a burial place.
It is the first piece of the promised land Abraham actually owns.
24: Abraham sends his servant back to his relatives. The servant prays for a sign at a well, and Rebekah offers water to him and his camels. She agrees to go and marries Isaac.
God guides ordinary events through prayer and kindness.
25: Abraham dies. Rebekah bears twins who struggle in the womb. Esau, hungry from hunting, sells his rights as firstborn to Jacob for a bowl of stew.
Esau trades something lasting for a moment's appetite.
26: In a famine God renews the promise to Isaac. He prospers, is envied, and keeps moving on and digging new wells instead of fighting.
The promise passes to the next generation. Isaac is a man of peace.
27: With Rebekah's help, Jacob disguises himself as Esau and tricks blind Isaac into giving him the firstborn's blessing. Esau plans to kill him, and Jacob flees.
God's plan moves forward even through deceit, but the family pays for it.
28: Fleeing, Jacob sleeps with a stone for a pillow and dreams of a stairway to heaven with angels going up and down. God repeats the promise to him. He names the place Bethel, "house of God".
God comes to Jacob when he is a fugitive. Jesus applies the image of the ladder to himself.
29: Jacob works seven years for Rachel. His uncle Laban tricks him into marrying her older sister Leah first, and he works seven more for Rachel. Leah bears four sons.
The deceiver is deceived. God notices unloved Leah.
30: Through Leah, Rachel and their maids, Jacob has eleven sons and a daughter. Rachel at last bears Joseph. Jacob grows rich in flocks despite Laban's tricks.
The twelve tribes of Israel begin in a troubled family.
31: Jacob slips away with his family. Rachel steals her father's household idols. Laban catches up, and they make a pact of peace.
God protects Jacob as he promised at Bethel.
32: Afraid to meet Esau, Jacob prays and sends gifts ahead. That night a man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob will not let go without a blessing and is renamed Israel.
Prayer can be a struggle. Jacob leaves limping and blessed.
33: Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him and weeps. Jacob settles near Shechem.
Forgiveness between brothers is possible after years of hatred.
34: Shechem violates Jacob's daughter Dinah and then asks to marry her. Her brothers Simeon and Levi trick the men of the city and slaughter them.
The Bible records the sins of its own heroes without excusing them.
35: Jacob has his household bury their foreign gods and returns to Bethel, where God confirms his new name. Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin. Isaac dies.
Coming back to God means getting rid of idols.
36: A list of the family and chiefs of Esau, the people of Edom.
God kept his promise to bless Esau too.
37: Jacob favours Joseph and gives him a special coat. Joseph's dreams anger his brothers, who sell him to traders and show their father the coat dipped in blood.
Joseph, betrayed and sold for silver, is a figure of Christ.
38: Judah fails in his duty to his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar. Disguised, she conceives by him. When exposed, Judah admits, "She is more righteous than I."
Tamar appears in the family tree of Jesus. God works through messy lives.
39: Joseph prospers as a slave in Egypt. His master's wife tries to seduce him. He refuses and runs, is falsely accused, and is put in prison.
"How could I do this great evil and sin against God?" Joseph stays faithful when no one would know.
40: Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. Both come true. The cupbearer forgets him.
Joseph keeps serving while he waits. God's timing is not ours.
41: Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows and seven thin ones. Joseph explains: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Pharaoh puts him in charge of all Egypt.
God raises the humble at the right time and uses Joseph to save many lives.
42: Famine sends Joseph's brothers to Egypt. He recognises them, but they do not know him. He tests them and keeps Simeon until they bring Benjamin.
Their guilt over Joseph surfaces after twenty years. Conscience does not forget.
43: When the grain runs out, Judah guarantees Benjamin's safety and Jacob lets him go. Joseph feasts them and is moved to tears at the sight of his brother.
Judah, who once sold a brother, now takes responsibility for one.
44: Joseph has his cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. When it is found, Judah offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place.
The brothers have changed. Judah is ready to give himself for another.
45: Joseph cannot hold back and reveals himself. He tells his terrified brothers not to be distressed: God sent him ahead to save lives. He sends for his father.
Joseph forgives completely and sees God's hand in what was done to him.
46: God tells Jacob in a vision not to be afraid to go. The family, seventy people, moves to Egypt, and Jacob embraces Joseph.
Israel enters Egypt as a family. It will leave as a nation.
47: Jacob blesses Pharaoh, and the family settles in the land of Goshen. Joseph manages the famine. Jacob asks to be buried in Canaan.
Jacob calls his life a pilgrimage. His heart is in the promised land.
48: Jacob adopts Joseph's two sons and, crossing his hands, gives the greater blessing to the younger.
Again and again in Genesis, God chooses the one nobody expected.
49: On his deathbed Jacob speaks over each of his twelve sons. Of Judah he says the sceptre will not depart from him until the one comes to whom it belongs.
The promise of a king from Judah points to David and finally to Christ.
50: Jacob is buried in Canaan. The brothers fear revenge, but Joseph says, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." Joseph dies, asking that his bones be carried home one day.
God can bring good out of human evil. This line sums up the whole story of Joseph.
